# Reproduction harness

A harness is a script that makes the reported failure happen and says so with an
exit code. It is the acceptance test for the fix: it fails against the target
branch, passes against the fix branch, and the reviewer reads its output.
Screenshots are evidence; the assertion is the verdict.

## Where it lives

`.repro/<TICKET>/` inside the worktree — `repro.mjs`, `case-<name>.png`,
`repro.console.txt` if the console matters. Before writing anything there:

```bash
grep -qxF '.repro/' .git/info/exclude || echo '.repro/' >> .git/info/exclude
mkdir -p .repro/<TICKET>
```

`.git/info/exclude` is shared by every worktree of the repository and is not
committed, which is the point: nothing under `.repro/` can be staged, appear in a
diff, or reach a merge request. Evidence is attached to the ticket and the pull
request, never committed.

One thing does travel: the **source of `repro.mjs`**, copied into the RCA under
*Reproduction* so the RCA stands on its own for whoever reads it next (see
*Handing the reproduction on*). Only the source — never a screenshot, `state.json`
or console log — and only after you have read it through for anything that looks
like a credential. The template inlines none; a harness that does gets fixed, not
embedded.

## Environment and login

You stood this worktree's version of the app up yourself, from the repository's
`.prepcook/scripts.toml` — `setup`, `build`, `start`, `seed`, the commands the
orchestrator runs. It listens at `$PREPCOOK_APP_URL`, seeded with the project's test
data. Rebuilding and restarting it from the worktree's current files (the
manifest's `build`, then `start`) is how a harness is run
against a candidate change. Use the seeded data, and find records by what they
are called in the UI, never by an id you remember — ids differ per seed run.

The test login is in `$PREPCOOK_TEST_USER_EMAIL` and `$PREPCOOK_TEST_USER_PASSWORD`, plus
whatever else the seed wrote to `$PREPCOOK_ENV_OUT` and you exported. The template reads
them from the environment at run time; the values pass through no file, no log
line, no comment and no screenshot. If the app reports one of the project's
seed-error patterns (the playbook names them), or the seeded login cannot reach
what the seed should have given it, that is a seed problem, not something to work
around: say which and stop.

The template imports `playwright`. If the worktree cannot resolve it, install it
under `.repro/` so nothing in the project changes — `npm install --prefix .repro
playwright`, then `npx --prefix .repro playwright install chromium` once.
`$PREPCOOK_CHROMIUM_PATH`, when set, names a Chromium to use instead.

## Rules the template enforces

- **Log in once.** Save `storageState` to `.repro/<TICKET>/state.json` (mode 600)
  and reuse it for every case; re-login only when a case gets the login page.
- **Wait, then look.** `networkidle`, then a settle beat, before reading the DOM or
  clicking. A screenshot of a half-rendered page is evidence of nothing.
- **Selectors from reconnaissance.** Capture the rendered DOM of the page first and
  choose selectors from what is there. A guessed selector fails silently and turns a
  bug investigation into harness debugging.
- **One JSON line per case on stdout**, nothing else on stdout:
  `{"case":"b","expected":"","observed":"1mind","pass":false}`. Diagnostics go to
  stderr. No log files.
- **Exit non-zero when any case fails.** `/prepcook-fix` and `/prepcook-review` read the
  exit code; prose does not count.
- **Every case has a control** that must pass on the target branch, so a broken
  harness cannot masquerade as a reproduced bug.
- **Screenshot every case** to `.repro/<TICKET>/case-<name>.png` after it settles.

## When the failure is intermittent

A pass/fail harness cannot describe a bug that happens sometimes. Run one three
times, watch it pass three times, and you have measured nothing — which is how a
reproduction reports success while the customer keeps hitting the failure.

When the report says "sometimes", "intermittently", "every few days", or names a
window rather than an action, the harness measures a **rate**, not a verdict:

- **Fix N and the threshold before the first run.** How many trials, and what
  separation counts as reproduced. Choosing either afterwards is choosing the
  answer.
- **Run a control arm in the same session** — same app, same seed, a path you
  expect to be healthy — and report both rates. 3-in-20 on the subject means
  nothing until the control is 0-in-20.
- **One JSON line per trial**, with its arm:
  `{"case":"nightly-send","arm":"subject","trial":7,"observed":"timeout","pass":false}`.
  The rate is computed from the lines; it is never asserted in prose.
- **Exit non-zero when the subject's rate clears the threshold.** That is the
  reproduction. A single failing trial is evidence, not the verdict.
- **Say what you could not hold still** — time of day, concurrent load, queue
  depth, whatever else was running against the app. A rate without its conditions is a
  number.

## When you cannot make it fail

That is a result, and it is reported as one — never as "not on the target
branch's path", which is a different and much stronger claim.

Record how many trials, against what, over what period, and with what control.
State confidence low, and name what would raise it: more trials, a data shape
the seed lacks, a specific customer configuration, a correlation with
time or load that a longer run would surface. Put the one question that would
most change the answer to the reporter, in the same comment that reports the
attempt.

"I ran it forty times and it never failed, and here is what I could not rule
out" is worth more to whoever picks this up than a confident wrong cause.

## Running it

Foreground, bounded, never polled:

```bash
timeout 600 node .repro/<TICKET>/repro.mjs; echo "exit=$?"
```

Raise the Bash tool's own timeout to match, and keep the harness in the foreground so
its exit code is what you report.

Record the UTC time of the run in the RCA or the report, and the commit the app was
built from (`git rev-parse HEAD`).

## Reporting

On the ticket, through your tracker's MCP, with `REPRODUCTION:` alone as the first
line: the JSON lines verbatim, the mechanism in one paragraph, "the app at" the
target branch (or the fix branch) with the commit and the UTC time; screenshots
attached. That header is what `/prepcook-review` looks for, and a reproduction it cannot
find is reported as a missing one. Write it plainly enough for the reporter, who
reads the same comment. In the RCA: the same under *Reproduction*,
with the harness's source in a `<pre>` block — HTML-escaped, so `<`, `>` and `&`
in the script become `&lt;`, `&gt;` and `&amp;` — and the seed notes and kickoff
below under *Reproduce locally*.
Any question the harness cannot answer goes to the reporter in the ticket comment —
do not wait for the answer.

## Handing the reproduction on

The harness is half of a reproduction. The other half is the data it drives —
and whoever takes the ticket over starts from their own checkout, not this
worktree. Because the app is seeded by the project's own script, that half is
mostly reproducible already: their `seed` creates the same kind of records. The
RCA says which of them the failure depends on, so it stands on its own: the
harness's source and cases under *Reproduction*, and under *Reproduce locally*
what the harness relied on from the seed plus a kickoff prompt.

Write the seed notes from what you actually used, as of the last run. Names and
shapes, never ids — ids differ per seed run. Never credentials — not a password,
token, connection string or host, however it is encoded.

- **User** — which seeded login (by the role or name the seed gives it, never the
  value of a variable), and any permission or sharing the failure depends on.
- **Records** — the seeded records the harness opened or changed, by what they
  are called in the UI, and the field values the failure depends on.
- **Anything you created** — what, how (UI or API), and why the seed lacked it.
  This is what the next person has to recreate by hand.
- **Data the failure depends on** — described as a shape, not dumped: "a list
  shared with a second user who has since been removed". If it is customer data
  the seed cannot hold, say so plainly; the kickoff has to carry that.

Then the kickoff, in a `<pre>` block the reader copies whole, with the bracketed
parts filled in and nothing else changed:

```
Use the prepcook-repro skill. Reproduce [TICKET] in my local checkout.

Stand the app up the way .prepcook/scripts.toml says (setup, build, start, seed),
and read its address and test login from the environment the seed writes. Do
not ask me for the login and do not invent one; never write it into a file or
echo it back.

The seed notes at the end say which seeded records and which user the
reproduction relies on, and what was created by hand because the seed lacks
it. Recreate only the hand-made part, through the app's UI or API, and stop
and ask me before anything that needs a credential the seed did not export.

The harness is the script under Reproduction in this RCA. Save it, exactly as
it is there, as .repro/[TICKET]/repro.mjs, and add `.repro/` to
.git/info/exclude so it cannot be committed. Run it against [TARGET BRANCH] and
show me it failing; check out the fix branch, restart the app, run it again,
and show me it passing.

If it passes on [TARGET BRANCH], fails on the fix branch, or cannot run because
the notes name data my seed does not create, stop and tell me which. That is a
finding, not a setup problem to work around.

Finish with a numbered list of every step you needed me for and everything you
created, so the next person can do this without you.

SEED NOTES
[the seed notes, verbatim]
```

That prompt is also how a ticket changes hands. Someone taking it over reads the
RCA, pastes this, and has the failure in front of them before they read a line of
the diff.

## The template

`harness.template.mjs` beside this file is the starting point. Copy it to
`.repro/<TICKET>/repro.mjs`, fill in the cases, keep the structure. It verifies
certificates like a browser would; never add `ignoreHTTPSErrors` — a certificate
error on the app is a finding to report, not a flag to set.
